presenterNotes: Start with the core definition: a function is a relation where each input has exactly one output. Use the vending machine analogy.
For the vertical line test, physically draw a graph and pass a ruler vertically to show intersections.
Emphasize that the domain and range of a function depend on the context; real-world problems often restrict the domain to feasible values.
Encourage students to ask 'What depends on what?' when identifying independent and dependent variables.
title: Chapter 3.1 — Functions

explanation: A [[kw:relation]] is any set of ordered pairs. It connects inputs (x‑values) to outputs (y‑values).
A [[kw:function]] is a special relation where [[imp:each input has exactly one output]].
You can test a relation using ordered pairs, tables, mapping diagrams, or graphs.
The [[kw:vertical line test]]: If a vertical line crosses a graph at more than one point, the graph does NOT represent a function.
Remember: It's okay if two different inputs share the same output – that's still a function.

formulaCard.title: Vertical Line Test
notes: If a vertical line hits more than one point, the relation fails.
This works because a function has only one y‑value for each x‑value.
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{No vertical line intersects the graph more than once} \Rightarrow \text{function} $$

teacherCues: Write several ordered pairs on the board. Ask: 'Can an input have two different outputs? If so, is it a function?'
Draw a mapping diagram with arrows; emphasize that each input must have exactly one arrow.

discoveryHook.scenario: Think of a vending machine: you press a button (input) and get a specific snack (output). If pressing the same button sometimes gave different snacks, it would be broken! A function works the same way – each input must have exactly one output.

hints: It starts with 'f'.
It passes the vertical line test.
questions.prompt: A relation where each input has exactly one output is called a ___.

hints: Check if any x‑value appears more than once with different y‑values.
Look at input 8.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Input 8 has outputs 1 and 2, so it's not a function.

questions.prompt: The vertical line test is used on which representation of a relation? (one word)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The vertical line test is used on a graph.
hints: It involves drawing lines on a picture.
Not a table or set of ordered pairs.

confusionCorner.title: Repeated Outputs are Fine!
confusionCorner.body: A function can have the same output for multiple inputs. In Example A, both (0,6) and (1,6) are okay. The problem only occurs when the [[imp:same input]] gives different outputs.

blocks.title: Relations and Functions

steps: List the inputs: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2. None repeat.
Even though outputs 8 and 6 appear twice, inputs are all different.
Each input has exactly one output. So it IS a function.
examples.title: A – Checking Ordered Pairs

steps: Notice that −1 appears twice: once with output 0, once with output 1.
A function cannot give two different outputs for the same input.
Therefore, this relation is NOT a function.
examples.title: B – Spotting the Duplicate Input
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to your partner: Why does the input −1 having two different outputs break the function rule?

examples.title: C – Vertical Line Test
examples.prompt: A graph passes the vertical line test if every vertical line touches the graph at most once. A circle centered at the origin – is it a function?
steps: Imagine drawing a vertical line through the circle. It will intersect at two points (except at the edges).
Because a vertical line can hit the circle twice, it fails the test.
So the graph does NOT represent a function.

examples.title: A – Domain and Range from Points
steps: Domain: x‑values are 0, 1, 2, 3.
Range: y‑values are 8, 9, 10, 11.
No repeats; list them as the domain and range.
examples.prompt: Find the domain and range of the function {(0,8), (1,9), (2,10), (3,11)}.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do we write the domain as $ -2 \le x \le 4 $ instead of just the endpoints?
examples.prompt: The graph is a line segment from (−2,0) to (4,5). Find the domain and range.
examples.title: B – Domain and Range from a Continuous Graph
steps: The graph includes all x‑values between −2 and 4, not just the endpoints.
So domain is $ -2 \le x \le 4 $.
Similarly, y goes from 0 to 5, so range is $ 0 \le y \le 5 $.
Both are sets of specific discrete values.
examples.prompt: A function is given by the table: x: 2,4,6,8; y: 2.6,5.2,7.8,10.4. Find domain and range.
examples.title: C – Domain/Range from a Table

teacherCues: Draw a graph with points (1,2), (2,4), (3,6). Ask: 'What are the possible x‑values? The y‑values?'
Label domain as 'input set' and range as 'output set'.
blocks.title: Domain and Range of a Function

formulaCard.title: Domain and Range Notation
notes: For a set of points, list each value only once.
For a continuous graph, use inequality notation.

visuals.title: Finding Domain and Range from a Graph

rows.0: Continuous line from x=−2 to x=3

explanation: The [[kw:domain]] of a function is the set of all possible input values (x).
The [[kw:range]] is the set of all possible output values (y).
From a set of ordered pairs, list all x‑coordinates for the domain, and all y‑coordinates for the range.
From a graph, look at the horizontal extent for domain and vertical extent for range.
Domain and range can be written as lists, or as inequalities for continuous graphs.

discoveryHook.scenario: When you use a parking meter, the money you put in (input) determines the time you get (output). The domain is the set of all possible coins you can insert; the range is the set of possible minutes. Domain and range describe the boundaries of a function.

hints: Starts with 'd'.
Think of the horizontal extent on a graph.
questions.prompt: The set of all input values of a function is called the ___.
For the points (1,5), (2,5), (3,5), what is the range? (list the unique y‑values)
hints: All points have the same y‑value.
The range is just that single number.

questions.prompt: A graph is a horizontal line at y=3 from x=0 to x=5. What is the domain in inequality notation? (e.g., 0 ≤ x ≤ 5)
hints: Look at the smallest and largest x‑values.
The graph covers all x between 0 and 5.

confusionCorner.title: Listing Repeated Values Only Once
confusionCorner.body: If a function has points (1,2) and (2,2), the range is {2}, not {2,2}. Only unique values matter.

formulaCard.title: Identifying Variables in y = mx + b

explanation: The [[kw:independent variable]] is the input of a function; you can choose its value (often x).
The [[kw:dependent variable]] is the output; its value depends on the input (often y).
When a function is written as an equation, the dependent variable is isolated on one side.
In $ y = -3x + 12 $, $ y $ is the dependent variable, $ x $ is the independent variable.
You can identify them by asking: 'Which quantity depends on the other?'

confusionCorner.title: Which Variable is Which?
confusionCorner.body: The independent variable is the one you have control over or that you set. The dependent variable is the result. In $ y = 2x $, if you choose x, then y is calculated – so x is independent, y is dependent.

teacherCues: Write 'y = −3x + 12' and say: 'If x is number of gulps, y is juice left. Which variable depends on the other?'
Emphasize: The dependent variable is the output; it depends on the independent variable (input).
blocks.title: Independent and Dependent Variables

steps: Independent: x (number of gulps). Dependent: y (juice left).
Create input‑output table: when x=0, y=12; x=1, y=9; x=2, y=6; x=3, y=3; x=4, y=0.
examples.title: A – Juice Bottle
examples.prompt: $ y = -3x + 12 $ represents juice left after x gulps. Identify independent and dependent variables. If domain is {0,1,2,3,4}, find the range.

examples.title: B – Taxi Ride
steps: Independent: x (miles). Dependent: y (cost).
Domain: $ 0 \le x \le 20 $.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is the cost dependent on miles, not the other way around?
examples.prompt: $ y = 3.5x + 2.8 $ gives cost y for x miles. Identify variables. If you can travel at most 20 miles, what are the domain and range?
$ a = -4b + 14 $ gives avocados left after b batches. Identify variables. If domain is {0,1,2,3}, find range.
examples.title: C – Guacamole Left
steps: Independent: b (batches). Dependent: a (avocados left).

discoveryHook.scenario: When you fill a gas tank, the number of gallons you pump (input) determines the total cost (output). In math, the independent variable is the one you control; the dependent variable is the one that responds.

questions.prompt: In $ y = 5x - 7 $, the variable x is the ___ variable.
hints: It's the variable you input.
Starts with 'i'.

questions.prompt: The number of quarters you put in a meter affects the time you get. Which is the dependent variable? (time or quarters)
hints: Which one depends on the other?
The time you get depends on the quarters you put in.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Time is the dependent variable because it depends on the number of quarters.

hints: Which one can you choose?
The number of days late determines the rent.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Days late is the independent variable.
questions.prompt: For $ y = 25x + 500 $ (rent late fee), if x is days late, what is the independent variable? (days or rent)

explanation: Many everyday situations are modeled by functions: cost, distance, height, temperature.
The domain often has practical limits (e.g., time can't be negative, miles can't be negative).
The range is determined by plugging domain values into the function.
You can represent these functions as equations, tables, or graphs.
Use the context to decide whether the domain is discrete (specific numbers) or continuous (any number in an interval).

examples.prompt: The table shows savings balance y after x months. Write the function as ordered pairs. Identify domain and range.
examples.title: A – Savings Account

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does the domain end at about 2.5 seconds?
examples.title: B – Projectile Height
examples.prompt: The graph of a projectile's height h (ft) vs. time t (sec) is a parabola opening down from t=0 to t=2.5. Approximate domain and range.
steps: Domain is the time interval from launch to landing: approximately $ 0 \le t \le 2.5 $.
Range is the height from 0 ft up to the maximum (approx. 25 ft).
So range is $ 0 \le h \le 25 $.

examples.title: C – Hardcovers and Softcovers
steps: Domain and range depend on realistic quantities.
examples.prompt: $ 1.5x + 0.5y = 12 $ represents buying x hardcover and y softcover books. Solve for y, then list three possible ordered pairs.

blocks.title: Real-Life Applications of Functions

confusionCorner.body: In the savings example, you can't check the balance after 1.5 months if it's only recorded monthly. So the domain is discrete {0,1,2,3,4}. For the projectile, time is continuous, so the domain is an interval $0 \le t \le 2.5$.
confusionCorner.title: Discrete vs. Continuous Domain

discoveryHook.scenario: Your savings grow each month, a taxi fare increases with distance, a projectile's height changes over time – these are all functions describing the world around you. Understanding domain and range helps you know the limits of these real-life situations.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: If only whole hours are allowed, the domain is discrete.
hints: Can you park for 1.5 hours if the fee structure only counts full hours?
Think of the savings month example.
questions.prompt: If a function gives the cost of parking for h hours, and hours must be whole numbers, is the domain discrete or continuous?

hints: It's the output.
Starts with 'd'.
questions.prompt: In the projectile graph, the height depends on time, so height is the ___ variable.

hints: Solve for y.
questions.prompt: For the bookstore equation $ 1.5x + 0.5y = 12 $, if x=6, what is y?

teacherCues: Show a table of savings over months. Ask: 'If the balance is a function of the month, what's the domain?'
Guide students to write ordered pairs and plot them.

confusionCorner.body: Domain is always about inputs (x), range about outputs (y). In an equation $ y = f(x) $, the x‑values you plug in are the domain, the y‑values you get out are the range.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Mix Up Domain and Range

examples.title: A – Blueprint for Ordered Pairs
examples.prompt: Use the blueprint to determine if {(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)} is a function. Find domain and range.
steps: Understand: Ordered pairs given. Task: function test, then domain/range.
Solve: Inputs 1,2,3 unique → yes, it's a function. Domain={1,2,3}, Range={2,4,6}.
Conclude: The relation is a function because each x has exactly one y. Domain and range listed.

examples.prompt: A graph is a V‑shape opening up, vertex at (0,0). Is it a function? What are the domain and range?
steps: Understand: Graph of $ y = |x| $. Task: function test, domain/range.
Solve: No vertical line hits more than once → function. Domain: all real numbers. Range: $ y \ge 0 $.
Conclude: It's a function; domain is $ (-\infty, \infty) $, range is $ [0, \infty) $.
examples.title: B – Blueprint for Graph
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How does the vertical line test confirm it's a function?

steps: Understand: Equation given, context limits x. Task: variables, domain, range.
Solve: Independent x (miles), dependent y (cost). Domain $ 0 \le x \le 20 $. Range: evaluate at endpoints → $ 2.8 \le y \le 72.8 $.
Conclude: Cost depends on miles; domain and range are those intervals.
examples.title: C – Blueprint for Real‑World Equation
examples.prompt: $ y = 3.5x + 2.8 $ represents taxi cost. Identify variables, domain, and range if you travel up to 20 miles.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Working with Functions

hints: Starts with 'U'.
It's where you identify the representation and task.
questions.prompt: In the blueprint, what is the first phase?

hints: Not two or more.
The definition of a function.
questions.prompt: In the Solve phase for a function test, you check that each input has exactly ___ output.
For the set {(0,5),(1,6),(2,7)}, what is the domain? (list numbers separated by commas, e.g., 0,1,2)
hints: List all the first numbers of each pair.
Order doesn't matter.

discoveryHook.scenario: Functions can be represented in many ways – tables, graphs, equations, words. The Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint helps you approach any function problem systematically: figure out what's being asked, apply the right test or calculation, and interpret the answer in context.

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Walk through a function identification problem using the blueprint.
Emphasize: 'Understand' determines whether you are testing for a function, finding domain/range, or identifying variables.

explanation: The blueprint for functions: [[imp:Understand]] – What representation is given? What is being asked (function test, domain/range, variables)?
[[imp:Solve]] – Use the appropriate method: check inputs/outputs for function test, list or read values for domain/range, identify dependent/independent from context.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the result clearly. If a set is a function, say yes and explain why. Give domain and range using proper notation.

rows.1: Identify the representation (ordered pairs, graph, table, equation). Determine the task.
Apply function definition / vertical line test / find inputs & outputs / identify variables.
Answer the question: 'It is/is not a function because...' or list domain/range, etc.

notes: Check all inputs for duplicates with different outputs.
For graphs, use the vertical line test.
